stories.headline: S&P 500 TUMBLES 3.72% TO 6,910, NASDAQ 100 SINKS 5.63% TO 25,029 AS AI-CAPEX ROUT DEEPENS
stories.body: The S&P 500 dropped 3.72% to 6,910 and the Nasdaq 100 fell 5.63% to 25,029, the sharpest single-session declines of the month and a steep acceleration from Thursday's 2% slide, as the tech-led selloff that began in early November widened further.
stories.explain: The Nasdaq 100's loss running more than 50% worse than the S&P 500's is the signature of a narrow, valuation-driven unwind rather than a broad macro shock: the index's heaviest weights are the AI hyperscalers and chipmakers whose share prices embed years of assumed data-center revenue growth, so any doubt about that growth compresses their multiples far more than it hits the diversified S&P. With the Nasdaq already down double digits from its October high, today's move confirms investors are repricing AI capital-spending plans rather than reacting to a single day's headline.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD FALLS 14 BPS TO 4.91% AS TREASURIES RALLY INTO THE EQUITY ROUT
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slid 14 basis points to 4.91% even as the Fed's implied odds of a December hike rose, a combination that marks today as a growth scare rather than an inflation scare, with bond buyers treating Treasuries as the haven trade against the AI-led stock slide.
stories.explain: Yields usually rise alongside firmer hike odds, since a more hawkish path lifts the short-rate component of the curve; today's drop instead shows a flight-to-quality bid overwhelming that effect, as investors dump richly-valued equities and buy duration to hedge a slowing-growth scenario. That combination — stocks down hard, yields down too — tells a different story than a hot-inflation selloff: traders are pricing weaker forward earnings and GDP, not a Fed forced to tighten into strong growth, which is why the curve rallied on a day risk assets were pummeled.

stories.headline: DECEMBER HIKE ODDS NEAR 88% ON PREDICTION MARKETS AS OCT. PCE LOOMS NOV. 25
stories.body: Fed funds futures and prediction markets now put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting near 88%, up from roughly 77% a day earlier and 28% in mid-August, with the funds rate still at 3.75%-4.00%; the Oct. core PCE report on Nov. 25 and the November jobs report on Dec. 4 are the final inputs before the decision.
stories.explain: A jump of more than ten points in implied hike odds in a single day reflects traders pulling forward their inflation-persistence view faster than any one data release can explain, which usually means positioning catching up to a string of recent prints rather than one new shock. Because both the core PCE and payrolls reports land in the eight days before the meeting, either one has the mechanical power to swing that 88% figure sharply — a hot PCE print would cement the hike, while a soft jobs number could reopen the debate even this late in the cycle.

stories.headline: GOLD EDGES UP 0.17% TO $3,539, WTI CRUDE ADDS 0.76% TO $84 AS HAVEN FLOWS DIVERGE
stories.body: Gold rose a modest 0.17% to roughly $3,539 an ounce and WTI crude gained 0.76% to about $84 a barrel, both far calmer than the equity rout, while the dollar index was essentially flat at 103.84 (+0.05%).
stories.explain: Gold's muted move despite a sharp risk-off day shows the haven bid going overwhelmingly into Treasuries rather than bullion today, likely because falling yields already do most of gold's job of lowering the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset, leaving less incremental demand for gold specifically. A flat dollar alongside falling yields is also notable: normally lower U.S. rates would pressure the dollar versus other currencies, so DXY holding steady suggests other major economies are seeing comparable safe-haven demand for their own currencies today.

stories.headline: HUANG'S CLOSED-DOOR HOUSE TESTIMONY CONFIRMED FOR DEC. 1, NVIDIA GC TETER TO FOLLOW DEC. 2
stories.body: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned Nov. 12 amid national-security concerns about his ties to a businesswoman U.S. intelligence suspects of links to Chinese espionage, is confirmed for a closed-door, transcribed interview before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China select committees on Dec. 1, with Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter following Dec. 2.
stories.explain: A transcribed interview is negotiated privately between committee staff and counsel with no public broadcast and no subpoena deadline, which is why these dates slipped from an initially floated pre-Thanksgiving appearance to early December. For Nvidia shareholders already absorbing today's Nasdaq-led selloff, the lingering leadership vacuum compounds the AI-capex anxiety: a chipmaker at the center of the data-center buildout trading without a permanent CEO or resolved national-security question adds idiosyncratic risk on top of the sector-wide growth scare.

stories.headline: AI DATA-CENTER SPENDING DOUBTS WIDEN NASDAQ'S UNDERPERFORMANCE VERSUS S&P
stories.body: The gap between today's 5.63% Nasdaq 100 decline and the S&P 500's 3.72% drop underscores a selloff concentrated in AI infrastructure names, as investors increasingly question whether hyperscalers' data-center capital spending will generate profits fast enough to justify current valuations.
stories.explain: When a cap-weighted tech index falls meaningfully more than a broad index, the arithmetic says a handful of mega-cap names are doing most of the damage — here, the chipmakers and cloud providers whose capital expenditure guidance has been the market's main AI-growth proxy all year. The mechanism investors are repricing is straightforward: AI capex is booked as depreciation against future revenue that has to materialize on a multi-year timeline, and any sign that timeline is slipping forces a markdown of expected returns on hundreds of billions in committed spending, which hits the Nasdaq's AI-heavy weighting far harder than the diversified S&P.

watchlist: Oct. core PCE inflation data — Nov. 25, the last major print before the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting; Oxford Economics projects headline PCE near 3.8% y/y
November jobs report — Dec. 4, landing four days before the FOMC decision
Fed's Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting — hike odds near 88% with the funds rate at 3.75%-4.00%
Jensen Huang's closed-door House testimony — Dec. 1, with Nvidia GC Tim Teter following Dec. 2
Hyperscaler AI capex guidance — watch for any cuts to 2027 data-center spending plans as the key catalyst for the Nasdaq's underperformance

deepDive.title: Reading the 88%: How Fed Funds Futures and Prediction Markets Actually Price a Rate Hike
content: Friday's brief flagged a striking number: the implied odds of a December hike jumped to 88%, up from 77% a day earlier and just 28% in mid-August. With the Oct. core PCE report landing Nov. 25 and payrolls on Dec. 4 as the last two inputs before the Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting, that 88% figure is about to get tested twice in nine days. But the number itself is worth unpacking, because 'the market thinks a hike is 88% likely' is a mechanical output of two different pricing instruments, each measuring something slightly different, and conflating them is one of the most common mistakes finance students make when reading Fed-watching coverage.

The workhorse instrument is the CME's FedWatch calculation, built from 30-day Fed funds futures. A futures contract settles against the average effective fed funds rate for its delivery month, so its price embeds the market's expected average rate over that month. Subtract the current effective rate from the futures-implied rate, divide by the size of a standard hike (25 bps), and you get the probability-weighted expectation: if futures imply an average rate 22 bps above today's 3.875% midpoint, the market is pricing roughly an 88% chance of a quarter-point move. Prediction markets like Kalshi or Polymarket arrive at a similar number through a completely different mechanism — a binary contract trading at 88 cents simply means traders are willing to pay 88 cents for a dollar if the hike happens, which converts directly to an 88% probability only if the market is liquid and arbitrage-free.

What gets missed is that both numbers measure positioning, not the Fed's actual reaction function, and they can be wrong in a specific, recurring way: they underweight low-probability, high-conviction scenarios that large institutional players hedge in options rather than futures. December 2018 is the classic case — fed funds futures priced only modest hike odds for that meeting, yet the FOMC still hiked and triggered the worst December for stocks since the Depression, because the committee was anchored to its own forecasts more than to market pricing. The lesson is that an 88% futures-implied probability is the market's best guess given available data, not a preview of the Fed's actual vote.

That gap matters directly for the next nine days. A hot core PCE print on Nov. 25 would push the implied probability toward the high-90s with little room left to move, while a soft November payrolls report on Dec. 4 — four days before the decision — has more room to swing the number down, since it would be the more recent and more Fed-weighted data point. Layer in today's growth-scare bond rally, where yields fell even as hike odds rose, and the setup gets genuinely two-sided: a Fed that hikes into a market already flashing slowdown signals in equities risks a policy-error narrative, which is exactly the kind of divergence between market pricing and committee intent that 2018 should make every student of this cycle watch for.
